title: Thinking in a Dish: How Lab-Grown Neurons Became the World's First Living Computers
author: Kenji Nakamoto
research_method: 1 cached file scanned (BCI research — adjacent, not directly reused) + 2 Exa semantic searches returning primary/near-primary sources (Nature Reviews Bioengineering, New Scientist, the original DishBrain Neuron paper PDF, FinalSpark). Within the 60k-token research cap; no review pass.
thesis_angle: Biocomputing has crossed from a single viral proof-of-concept (neurons learning Pong in 2022) into an actual product category by 2025-2026: Cortical Labs shipping the CL1 'body-in-a-box' and FinalSpark renting cloud access to living organoids. The story is no longer 'can brain cells compute?' but 'what is a living computer actually good for, and how much of the hype is real?' — the honest answer being that these systems learn strikingly fast and sip energy, yet still play games far below human level and remain poorly understood even by their makers.

statistics.claim: The DishBrain system that first demonstrated neurons learning to play Pong was built from clusters of more than 800,000 living human and mouse brain cells grown on a high-density multi-electrode array.
statistics.source: New Scientist (reporting on Cortical Labs); original figure from Kagan et al., 'In vitro neurons learn and exhibit sentience when embodied in a simulated game-world,' Neuron
statistics.verification_flag: VERIFIED — the 800,000+ figure appears both in New Scientist (Feb 2026) and traces to the peer-reviewed 2022 Neuron paper (DishBrain). Strong, citable.

statistics.claim: In the original DishBrain experiments, cultured neurons showed apparent learning within five minutes of real-time Pong gameplay — a change in goal-directed firing not seen in control cultures.
statistics.source: Kagan, B. J. et al., 'In vitro neurons learn and exhibit sentience when embodied in a simulated game-world,' Neuron (peer-reviewed, primary source)
statistics.verification_flag: VERIFIED — direct from the primary Neuron paper PDF. Note the paper's use of the word 'sentience' is contested framing; cite the learning-time claim, not the sentience claim, without caveat.

statistics.claim: In a February 2026 demonstration, a Cortical Labs neuronal chip using only about a quarter as many neurons as the Pong setup (~200,000) was taught to play Doom in roughly a week — by an independent developer, Sean Cole, using a new Python interface rather than years of specialist lab work.
statistics.source: New Scientist (Alex Wilkins), quoting Cortical Labs
statistics.verification_flag: VERIFIED via New Scientist. The '~a quarter as many neurons' is stated directly; the ~200,000 figure is my arithmetic from the 800,000 Pong baseline — present as 'about a quarter' or '~200,000' clearly derived, not as an independently sourced count.

statistics.claim: FinalSpark's Neuroplatform offers 24/7 remote cloud access to living brain organoids and has accumulated over 30 terabytes of recorded neuronal activity data, which it makes available to researchers for free.
statistics.verification_flag: COMPANY SELF-REPORTED (marketing page) — accurate as a description of the offering and the 30 TB figure, but it is a vendor claim, not independently audited. Frame as 'FinalSpark says.'

statistics.claim: Cortical Labs' CL1 is a commercially available platform that couples in-vitro neural cultures with a closed-loop, real-time electrical interface and an integrated life-support perfusion circuit — described in Nature Reviews Bioengineering as a 'body-in-a-box' making biological neural computation a shippable device rather than a one-off lab rig.
statistics.source: Kagan, B. J., 'The CL1 as a platform technology to leverage biological neural system functions,' Nature Reviews Bioengineering 3, 724-725
statistics.verification_flag: VERIFIED — peer-reviewed journal (Nature Reviews Bioengineering, Sept 2025 issue). Note the author is affiliated with Cortical Labs, so it is a platform-advocacy piece, not an independent evaluation.

statistics.claim: A central promised advantage of biological computing is energy: neurons are argued to process information with dramatically less power than digital silicon (figures on the order of a million-fold are commonly cited by the field).
statistics.verification_flag: UNVERIFIED PRECISION — the Exa snippet confirmed FinalSpark asserts neurons 'compute information with much less energy' than digital systems, but the specific ~1,000,000x multiplier is a widely-repeated field talking point I could NOT pin to a controlled benchmark within budget. Do NOT cite an exact multiplier as measured fact; frame as 'proponents claim' / 'orders of magnitude.'

expert_quotes.quote: Yes, it's alive, and yes, it's biological, but really what it is being used as is a material that can process information in very special ways that we can't recreate in silicon.
expert_quotes.name: Brett Kagan
expert_quotes.verification_flag: VERBATIM from New Scientist (Feb 2026). Kagan is the lead figure behind DishBrain — note the vested interest when quoting.

expert_quotes.quote: What's exciting here is not just that a biological system can play Doom, but that it can cope with complexity, uncertainty, and real-time decision-making. That's much closer to the kinds of challenges future biological or hybrid computers will need to handle.
expert_quotes.name: Andrew Adamatzky
expert_quotes.affiliation: University of the West of England, Bristol (unconventional computing researcher)
expert_quotes.verification_flag: VERBATIM from New Scientist. An independent outside expert (not Cortical Labs) — good for balance.

expert_quotes.quote: [Doom] is a significant level up from playing Pong — but there is still a lot we don't understand about how these neurons are playing the game, such as how the neurons know what is expected of them or how they can 'see' the screen with no eyes.
expert_quotes.name: Steve Furber
expert_quotes.affiliation: University of Manchester (computer engineer, SpiNNaker neuromorphic project)
expert_quotes.verification_flag: LIGHTLY PARAPHRASED / STITCHED from two adjacent New Scientist sentences (the 'significant level up' and the 'lot we don't understand' points). The bracketed portion is a paraphrase — if quoting verbatim, split into two shorter direct quotes or attribute as reported. This is the strongest source for the skeptical/counterargument section.

counterargument.claim: The strongest skeptic's case: these are captivating demos, not useful computers. The Doom-playing culture performed only better than a randomly-firing player and 'far below the performance of the best human players' (New Scientist), and even the field's own leaders concede they don't fully understand HOW the neurons accomplish the task (Furber). Kagan himself cautions it 'isn't useful to compare the chips with human brains.' Add the unresolved ethical weight of computing on living human-derived neural tissue, the vendor-sourced nature of the energy and data claims, and the fact that no biocomputer performs any economically valuable task today — and the honest read is that biocomputing in 2026 is an important scientific frontier whose commercial value is still speculative, closer to the transistor in 1948 than to a product.
counterargument.verification_flag: Analytical synthesis grounded in the cited New Scientist quotes and stats; present explicitly as the article's counterargument.

recent_news.item: February 2026: Cortical Labs' brain-cell chips learned to play Doom in about a week, programmed via a new Python interface by an independent developer — a marked accessibility leap from the years-long specialist effort behind the 2021-22 Pong demo.

2025: The Cortical Labs CL1 was profiled in Nature Reviews Bioengineering as a shippable platform technology (closed-loop culture + life-support perfusion), signaling biocomputing's move from bespoke lab rigs toward a commercial device category.

unverified_claims_flagged: The exact energy-efficiency multiplier of neurons vs. silicon (~1,000,000x is a field talking point, not a benchmark I could confirm — frame as 'orders of magnitude, proponents claim').
The ~200,000-neuron figure for the Doom chip is derived from '~a quarter of 800,000,' not independently sourced.
FinalSpark's '30 TB' and '24/7 remote organoid access' are company self-reported marketing claims, not independently audited.
The DishBrain paper's 'sentience' language is contested in the neuroscience community; use the 'learning' framing, avoid asserting sentience.
